Hook: On the thirteenth of October 1908, a German chemist named Fritz Haber filed a patent on, in his words, the synthesis of ammonia from its elements. The elements were in the air. Four fifths of the air we breathe is nitrogen, and nitrogen is what every crop is hungriest for. But almost no plant can take it from the air, because the two atoms of a nitrogen molecule are held together by one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. Farmers had to bring nitrogen to their fields, as manure or as mined nitrate.

Haber's trick was to force nitrogen to combine with hydrogen. One molecule of nitrogen and three of hydrogen, squeezed to hundreds of atmospheres and heated over an iron catalyst, become two molecules of ammonia, which plants can use. Haber did it on a laboratory bench. It took an engineer, Carl Bosch, at the chemical company BASF, to build steel vessels that could hold the pressure at industrial scale, around 1913. Both won the Nobel Prize. In America today the hydrogen comes from natural gas, the dominant feedstock, as the US Geological Survey puts it.

In 1950 the world made about 5 million tonnes of nitrogen in ammonia. In 2025, about 160 million. Over the same century the number of people on Earth went from about 1.7 billion, when Haber filed his patent, to over eight billion. And the world's farmers now spread about 71 kilograms of nitrogen on each hectare of cropland, against about 9 in 1961.

Ammonia is one branch of a much bigger tree. The same natural gas gives up methane, which becomes the hydrogen for ammonia and fertilizer, and ethane, which becomes ethylene, which is strung together into polyethylene, one of the most common plastics: bags, bottles, films, the lining of a carton. From a few molecules of gas and oil, the chemical industry makes almost everything else: plastics, paints, fibres, fertilizers, detergents and medicines.

It is one of the largest industries in the world, and one of the least seen. Industry, Built. Part twelve: chemicals. How does a molecule of gas become a thousand products, and where in the chain is the money?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: a cracker for forty years.

Play it yourself. It is 2012. You run a chemical company, and you are about to build a steam cracker, the furnace at the root of the plastics industry: 1.5 million tonnes of ethylene a year, about 6 billion dollars, and a life of forty years. You can build it in Texas, and feed it ethane, a gas that comes out of the ground with natural gas, now pouring from America's shale fields and priced like natural gas. Or in Europe, near your customers, and feed it naphtha, a light oil from refineries, priced like crude. Ethylene is sold around the world at one price, set by the dearest crackers still needed to supply it, naphtha crackers in Asia, plus a bit more when plants are full. Pause, and choose.

Here is what a tonne of ethylene would have cost each plant to make, year by year, with the real prices of gas and oil. The world price, set by the dearest crackers. The European cracker on naphtha: it is one of those dear crackers, so the price barely covers its costs. And the Texas cracker on ethane: hundreds of dollars a tonne cheaper, every single year, in 2013 almost a thousand dollars. That gap is its margin: about 418 dollars a tonne even in a bad year like 2016, against 137 in Europe.

Now add it up, after 150 million dollars a year of fixed costs. The Texas cracker earned back its 6 billion dollars by 2020, and about 12 billion by 2026. The European cracker earned barely enough to keep running, and nothing like enough to pay for itself. In this industry, the choice that matters most is made once, when you pick the site and the feedstock, and it decides the next forty years.

And that is what the industry did. From 2013, America built the first new crackers in more than a decade, raising its capacity from about 27 to almost 40 million tonnes of ethylene a year by 2020. Europe has been closing them: Dow will shut its cracker at Böhlen in Germany by the end of 2027. And the one big new cracker in Europe, INEOS's in Antwerp, was built to run on American ethane, carried across the ocean in special ships. If you cannot move the plant to the gas, you move the gas.
Tree: Chapter two. Three raw materials, a thousand products.

The chemical industry starts from very few raw materials. Natural gas, crude oil and salt. From them it makes a handful of building blocks, in enormous quantities: ammonia and methanol from the methane in gas; ethylene, propylene and butadiene from ethane or from naphtha; benzene and xylenes from oil; and chlorine and caustic soda by passing electricity through salt water. The building blocks are joined into materials: fertilizers; solvents and glues; polyethylene from ethylene; PVC from ethylene and chlorine; polypropylene; synthetic rubber; polyester and nylon. And the materials become things: crops, paint, bags and bottles, pipes, car parts, tyres and clothes. Every step down the tree adds value, and, as we will see, the money is not spread evenly along it.

How big is it? American chemical makers sold about 901 billion dollars' worth of products in 2022, by the Census Bureau's count. The largest group is the basic chemicals at the root of the tree, about 298 billion dollars, petrochemicals among them. Then medicines, about 234 billion, which this series leaves for its own part. Then plastics and rubber, soaps and cosmetics, paints, and fertilizers. This part follows the industrial chemistry: the basic chemicals, the plastics and fertilizers made from them, the gases, and the speciality products at the end of the chain.
Cracker: Here is the plant this whole industry turns on. Ethane, or naphtha, is mixed with steam and sent through tubes inside a furnace, heated red hot. For a fraction of a second the molecules shake themselves apart. An ethane molecule loses two hydrogen atoms and becomes ethylene, with a double bond that makes it eager to join other molecules. The gas is cooled at once, so the cracking stops, then compressed, chilled, and separated in tall columns into ethylene, propylene, hydrogen, methane and the rest. A world-scale cracker is one of the largest and most expensive single machines in industry, and it runs flat out, day and night, for decades.

What comes out depends on what goes in. Crack a tonne of ethane, and about 81 per cent of it comes out as ethylene, by the government's engineering figures. Most of the rest is hydrogen and methane, burned as fuel. Crack a tonne of naphtha, and only about 39 per cent is ethylene. The rest is a little of everything: propylene, about 15 per cent, butadiene for rubber, benzene and the other aromatics for fibres and resins, and fuel. So an ethane cracker is an ethylene machine, and a naphtha cracker is a supermarket: more complicated, more flexible, and, as we are about to see, usually dearer.

Now the money, for a tonne of ethylene at 2026's prices, in this series' model, drawn to one scale. In Texas, the ethane for a tonne costs about 262 dollars. Sell the hydrogen and methane, add the fuel the furnace burns and the other running costs, and a tonne costs about 360 dollars. In Europe, on naphtha, the feed for a tonne of ethylene costs about 1,858 dollars, because it takes more than two and a half tonnes. The by-products are worth a great deal, and they bring most of it back. But the furnace burns European gas, and after everything a tonne costs about 1,097 dollars. The lesson of the cracker: the feedstock and the fuel are most of the cost, and the cheapest molecules win.
Shale: To see why America's crackers are so cheap to run, go underground. In the 2000s, drillers learned to turn a well sideways inside a layer of shale and crack the rock open with water and sand under pressure, freeing gas that had been locked in it. Much of that gas is what the industry calls wet: mostly methane, but carrying ethane, propane and butane with it. At a gas processing plant the heavier molecules are separated out. The methane goes into the pipeline, to homes and power stations. The ethane can go to a cracker. And when ethane is too cheap to bother, producers simply leave it in the gas and sell it as fuel, which ties its price to the price of natural gas.

Here is what shale did to the supply of ethane. For a quarter of a century, America produced around half a million barrels a day, 314 thousand in 1981, by the Energy Information Administration's count. Then the shale gas came, and the ethane came with it. By Aug 2026, about 3,361 thousand barrels a day, about 3 times the average as recently as 2015. So much that America now sells it abroad, by pipeline and in specially built ships: exports started in 2014 and reached about 794 thousand barrels a day.

Gas, unlike oil, is expensive to move across oceans: it has to be chilled into a liquid and shipped. So it has no single world price. Until about 2008, America, Europe and Asia paid roughly the same. Then shale flooded the American market, and its price fell away from the rest. In 2013, gas cost 3.73 dollars per million British thermal units in America, 11.19 in Europe and 17.34 in Asia. And in 2022, when Russia cut off most of its gas to Europe, Europe paid 38 dollars, about 6 times America's 6.52. Every cracker and every ammonia plant in Europe paid it too.

Put those prices through the Works' cracker, and you see the shale advantage open up. In the early 2000s, ethane in Texas and naphtha in Europe made ethylene for about the same cost: on average, the two were within 29 dollars a tonne of each other. From 2010, the gap averaged about 608 dollars a tonne, in a product that sells for around a thousand. It is not a better machine. It is the same machine with cheaper molecules, and an advantage that lasts as long as American gas stays cheap and stranded on its own continent.
Cycle: Part 6 of this series showed how an industry that builds slowly, and orders by today's price, swings. Petrochemicals are the purest case. Picture six companies, three with crackers running, in a year when the plants are full and margins are fat. Every one of them sees the same numbers, and three decide to build. A cracker takes years. While they are being built, demand keeps growing, the plants stay full, and the margins stay fat, which only seems to prove the decision right. Then they all start up within a year or two of each other. Capacity jumps far ahead of demand, the plants run part-empty, and the margin collapses. Now nobody builds. Demand grows into the new capacity, year by year, until the plants are full again, the margins are fat again, and everyone sees the same numbers.

Here is the real thing, as far back as the Federal Reserve's figures go. This is how much of America's chemical capacity was in use each year, from 1948. It covers medicines and soaps as well as petrochemicals, so it averages a lot out. Even so, it swings. The deepest troughs: 1975, 1982, 2001, 2009 and 2013. The worst was 2009, when only 67 per cent of the capacity was used. And 2021, when demand came back from the pandemic faster than plants could follow, at 80 per cent.

The swings show up in prices. This is what American plants charged for plastic resins, polyethylene and the rest, since 1977. Year to year it jumps and falls by ten, twenty, even thirty per cent. The biggest rise in this record was 2021: 33 per cent in a single year. For a business that runs on margins of a few hundred dollars a tonne, those swings decide whether the year is a bonanza or a loss.

And they decide the profits. Here are four American makers of commodity chemicals, each bar a year of net income: Dow, LyondellBasell, Westlake and Olin. In 2021, with the plants full, the four made about 15 billion dollars between them. In 2025, with the plants less full and margins thin, they lost about 5 billion between them, counting the write-downs that come with bad years. Same plants, same people, four years apart. Not every chemical business lives like this. The next chapters go down other branches of the tree: fertilizer, which rides the price of gas; the gas companies, which almost never lose; and the paint makers.
Fertilizer: Chapter six. Fertilizer: gas into food.

Plants need three things from fertilizer above all. Nitrogen, which the air is full of, but in a form no crop can use until it is made into ammonia, and that takes natural gas. Phosphorus, which comes from phosphate rock, dug out of mines. And potassium, from potash, mined from the beds of ancient seas. So fertilizer is really two industries: a chemical one, which turns gas into nitrogen, and a mining one, which digs up the other two. American companies cover both: CF Industries makes nitrogen; Mosaic mines phosphate and potash; Israel's ICL mines potash too. Nitrogen is the one used in the largest amounts, and the one with the most interesting economics, because its main raw material is gas.

Here is the chemistry Fritz Haber found and Carl Bosch scaled up. One molecule of nitrogen, from the air, and three of hydrogen, pressed together over an iron catalyst at hundreds of degrees and hundreds of atmospheres, make two molecules of ammonia. The hard part is the hydrogen. In plants like CF Industries', it is stripped from methane, natural gas, with steam, and more gas is burned to heat and squeeze the whole process. How much? CF's filing gives the numbers: it used 350 million million-Btu of gas in 2025 and made 10.1 million tons of ammonia: about 35 million Btu in every ton. At the 3.31 dollars CF paid for its gas, that is about 114 dollars a ton. At twelve dollars, about what Europe paid in 2025, it is about 415. Ammonia is, in effect, natural gas in a different form.

So the cost of ammonia rises and falls with gas. This is the gas in a ton of ammonia, at American prices and at European prices, year by year. Before shale they were close. After it, Europe's was often two to five times America's. In 2022, the gas alone for a ton cost a European plant about 1,298 dollars. Ammonia itself sold on America's Gulf Coast for about 1,070, by the Geological Survey's figures. So European plants that bought gas at market prices lost money on every ton, and some stopped. CF closed one British plant in 2022 and stopped making ammonia at the other in 2023, because of the cost of gas, its filing says. An American plant paid about 225 dollars for the gas in the same ton.

Who makes it? The world made about 160 million tonnes of nitrogen as ammonia in 2025, the Geological Survey estimates. China, about 49 million. India and Russia, about 15 each. America, about 14. America has 38 ammonia plants, with 57 per cent of the capacity in Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas, next to the gas, and 88 per cent of what they make goes into fertilizer. Potash is a different map, because you can only mine it where the old seas left it. Canada is far ahead, with about 15 million tonnes, then Russia, China and Belarus. America mines only about 0.5 million tonnes, and imports about 5.6 million, 79 per cent of it from Canada.

And the money. These are the profits of CF Industries, which makes nitrogen, and of Mosaic, which mines phosphate and potash, since 2015. In 2022, with European producers priced out by their gas, CF earned about 3.3 billion dollars, on cheap American gas and a world price set by the expensive plants. It is the cracker story again, with a different molecule. Over the last five years, CF kept about 22 cents of every dollar of sales as profit, more than any other company in this part. Fertilizer is cyclical, but the cheapest producer in a world priced by the dearest does very well.
Intermission: An intermission: eighty years of the world's ammonia, in the Geological Survey's records. After the Second World War, about 2 million tonnes of nitrogen a year. By 1970, 39 million: the fertilizer that came with new seeds and new farming around the world. It doubled again by the end of the 1980s. A dip in the early 1990s, as the Soviet Union broke up. And then a steady climb, to about 160 million tonnes in 2025. The gold underneath is America: about 24 per cent of the world's ammonia in 1950, about 9 per cent now, though its story has a twist.

Here is the twist. American ammonia grew for forty years, to about 15 million tonnes of nitrogen in 1980. Then, in the 2000s, American gas got dear. The gas in a ton of ammonia rose to about 308 dollars by 2005, and America's output fell by almost half, to 7.7 million tonnes in 2009, as plants shut or sat idle. Then shale gas made America one of the cheapest places on earth to make ammonia, and the plants came back: about 14 million tonnes in 2025. The industry follows its molecule.

The story so far. The chemical industry turns gas, oil and salt into a handful of building blocks, and those into almost everything. At its root is the cracker, a furnace that turns ethane or naphtha into ethylene. The feedstock is most of the cost, and the cheapest molecules win. Shale made America's ethane and gas the cheapest in the rich world. Everyone builds in the good years, so the bad years follow. And ammonia is natural gas in another form. Next: the businesses that do not cycle, Europe's shock, plastics, the harm, and the landscape.
Gases: Chapter seven. The plant at the fence.

The strangest business in chemicals sells air. Take a hundred molecules of air: seventy-eight are nitrogen, twenty-one oxygen, and about one argon. An air separation unit squeezes air, chills it until it turns liquid, colder than minus a hundred and eighty degrees, and distils it like crude oil in a refinery, because each gas boils at a different temperature. Out come nitrogen, to keep oxygen away from food, chips and chemicals; oxygen, for steelmaking, hospitals and glass; and argon, for welding and making chips. The same companies also make hydrogen, from natural gas, for refineries.

The gas reaches customers in three ways. In cylinders, for welders, laboratories and hospitals. As a liquid, by truck, into a tank at a food plant or a factory, on contracts of three to seven years. And for the largest customers, a steel mill, a refinery, a chemical or a chip plant, the gas company builds a plant right at the fence and pipes the gas in. Those on-site plants come with long contracts: 10 to 20 years at Linde, with minimum purchases and prices that rise with costs; 15 to 20 years at Air Products, their filings say. And because most of these gases are, in Linde's words, uneconomical to carry more than a few hundred miles, the plant nearest the customer has a large advantage.

Why do these contracts matter so much? Play it with the Works' model of a gas plant. The gas company spends about 400 million dollars on a plant at a steel mill's fence. The mill signs for 15 years: a fixed fee every year, and it pays for at least 80 per cent of the gas, whether it uses it or not. In a good year the mill takes everything, and the gas plant makes about 90 million dollars of cash. Now a recession: the mill cuts back to half. A plant selling gas by the tonne would lose half its income. Under the contract, the gas company still gets its fee and its minimum, and saves the electricity it no longer burns: about 94 million. Even if the mill stops altogether, the cash hardly moves. The customer carries the cycle. The gas company has, in effect, rented the mill a machine.

Here is what that looks like in the accounts. Dow, the commodity maker, swings from profit to loss and back. Linde, the largest industrial gas company in the world by its own account, made more profit every single year from 2019 to 2025, to about 6.9 billion dollars. Over five years Linde kept about 17 cents of every dollar of sales as profit, and Air Products about 17, against Dow's 3. Even Air Products' bad year proves the point: it lost money in fiscal 2025 after about 3 billion dollars of charges to walk away from big new energy projects, while its adjusted operating income, which leaves such charges out, reached about 3.2 billion the following year.

And in the prices. This is what American producers charged for petrochemicals since 2004: up, down, up, down, falling in 10 of the 21 years. And for industrial gases: falling in only 3, and ending at about 2.5 times where it started. Contracts that pass on costs, customers that cannot easily switch, and a product too costly to carry far make one of the steadiest businesses in chemicals. It is chemistry run like a utility.
Specialty: At the far end of the tree are the chemicals sold not by the tonne but by what they do. Take a can of paint. Inside, by Sherwin-Williams' own description: resins and latex, which form the film; pigments for colour; additives; solvents, often water; and the can. And much of it, the company says, comes from petrochemicals, notably propylene, straight from the crackers of chapter three. But you do not buy paint from a cracker. Sherwin-Williams sells it through 4,853 stores of its own in America, Canada and the Caribbean, to painting contractors and to people doing up their homes, tinted to order.

Here is the difference that makes, in one dollar of sales. When Dow sold a dollar of chemicals and plastics in 2025, the materials, energy and running of its plants cost it about 94 cents, leaving 6 cents for everything else. When Sherwin-Williams sold a dollar of paint, about 49 cents were left after the cost of making it. Out of that it pays for its stores, its salespeople and its brand. The customer is paying for colour, service and a name a painter trusts, not for tonnes of chemicals.

And when the price of its ingredients falls, a paint maker does not have to pass it on. Petrochemical prices since 2004: falling in 10 of the 21 years. Paint: falling in 3. When oil and propylene jump, paint prices follow them up; when they fall, paint mostly stays where it is, and the difference becomes margin.

Over five years, that shows. Sherwin-Williams and Ecolab, which sells cleaning and water treatment, kept about 10 cents of every dollar as profit; PPG about 8. LyondellBasell and Dow, about 6 and 3. But specialty is not a guarantee. IFF, which makes flavours and fragrances, lost money: it wrote down about 6 billion dollars of goodwill in three of those years, the premium it had paid for businesses it bought. A good business bought at too high a price is a bad investment.
Europe: Now the other side of the shale story. In 2019, European gas cost a few dollars per million Btu, more than America's but not wildly so. Then, as economies reopened after the pandemic and Russia cut the gas it sent west, the price exploded. In Aug 2022 it reached about 70 dollars, against about 9 in America. It came down, but it never went back. In Sep 2026, European gas still cost about 9 times as much as American gas. For an industry whose raw material and fuel is gas, that is not a shock that passes. It is a new map.

And here is what it did to how much chemistry Europe makes, by Eurostat's monthly count. Germany made about as much chemistry in 2021 as in 2015. Then the gas price rose, and output fell, and kept falling. By Sep 2026, German chemical output was about 23 per cent below 2021, as low as in the depths of the financial crisis in 2009. The European Union as a whole, about 21 per cent below. How much of the fall is weak demand, and how much is production moving to cheaper places, is still argued over. The plants that are closing tell part of the story.

On the map, it looks like this. In England, CF Industries closed its Ince fertilizer plant in 2022 and stopped making ammonia at Billingham in 2023, citing the cost of gas. In Germany, Dow will shut its cracker at Böhlen by the end of 2027. And in Antwerp, INEOS's new cracker, Europe's largest, slated to start in the second half of 2026, is built to run on ethane shipped from America. Europe's chemical industry is not disappearing; it still makes a great deal. But at the root of the tree, where the feedstock is most of the cost, the plants that close are in the place where the molecules are dear, and the plants that are built use molecules from where they are cheap.
Plastics: Chapter ten. Plastics, and where they go.

The largest product of the cracker is plastic. Ethylene molecules each carry a double bond between their two carbons. With the right catalyst, the double bonds open, and the molecules link hand to hand into a chain, thousands of units long. That is polyethylene. It leaves the plant as pellets, by the bag and the railcar, and becomes bottles, film, bags and pipes. Polypropylene, PVC and the rest are made the same way from other building blocks.

And the world makes a great deal of it. In 1950, about 2 million tonnes. By 2019, about 460 million tonnes a year, roughly 59 kilograms for every person on earth. It grew so fast that half of all the plastic made between 1950 and 2019 was made after 2005.

Most of it is used briefly and thrown away. In 2019 the world threw out about 353 million tonnes of plastic, by the OECD's count. Here is what became of it, each square one per cent. About half, 50 per cent, went into landfills. About 22 per cent was littered or dumped where it was not managed, which is how it reaches rivers and seas. 19 per cent was burned. And 9 per cent was recycled.

Over time, recycling has grown, from about 4 per cent of plastic waste in 2000 to 9 in 2019. But the pile it is a share of grew faster, so more plastic went to landfill, and more was mismanaged, every year. There is an economic reason recycling struggles. Recycled plastic has to compete with new plastic, and new plastic is made from gas and oil at the lowest-cost crackers in the world. Collecting, sorting and cleaning a mixed bale of used packaging costs money that the price of new resin does not always cover. Which is why the question of who pays for plastic waste has become a question for governments.
Harm: Chapter eleven. The state and harm.

Chemistry has a dark side. At midnight on the second of December 1984, gas escaped from Union Carbide's plant in Bhopal, in India: methyl isocyanate, used to make pesticides, which the Supreme Court of India called a lethal toxic poison. It drifted over the sleeping city. By the count before the court, 2,660 people died at once, and thirty to forty thousand were seriously injured; the court itself spoke of tens of thousands left impaired. In 1989 the court ordered Union Carbide to pay 470 million dollars to settle the claims.

The other kind of harm is slow. PFAS are a large family of chemicals built on chains of carbon atoms wrapped in fluorine. The bond between carbon and fluorine is among the strongest in chemistry, which is what makes them useful in non-stick and stain-proof coatings, waterproof fabrics and firefighting foam. It is also why they barely break down. They have spread into water supplies, and they have earned a nickname: forever chemicals.

How little is too much? In April 2024 the Environmental Protection Agency set a limit for the two best-known PFAS, PFOA and PFOS, in drinking water: 4 parts per trillion. Four parts per trillion is about four drops in 20 Olympic swimming pools. Measuring that little, and taking it out of a city's water, is expensive, and someone has to pay for it.

And the bills have arrived. In 2023, 3M agreed to pay American public water systems between 10.5 and 12.5 billion dollars over PFAS, and said it planned to stop making them. Chemours, DuPont and Corteva agreed to a fund of about 1.19 billion dollars. Next to them, Bhopal's 470 million dollars, in the money of 1989. This is the pattern of chemical harm. The products were sold, and the profits booked, decades before the bill; and the people who pay first are often people who never bought them. That is why governments set limits, and why a chemical company's filings carry pages of lawsuits.
Landscape: Here is the landscape, as of November 2026: the chemical companies that file annual accounts in America, by revenue and by how much of each dollar they kept over five years. The commodity makers: Dow, the largest, and LyondellBasell, at 3 and 6 cents in the dollar; Westlake, Olin, Eastman, Celanese, Huntsman, all in single digits, through a boom and a bust. The gas companies, Linde and Air Products, around 17 cents, the steadiest. Fertilizer: CF at 22, the highest here, thanks to cheap American gas; Mosaic and ICL near ten. And the specialty makers, Sherwin-Williams, Ecolab and PPG around eight to ten, with IFF, after its write-downs, and Chemours, which shares the PFAS bill, at the bottom. The pattern of the whole part: the money is not in the size of the plant, it is in the price of the molecule going in and the hold on the customer coming out.

And what to watch. Europe's gas: in Sep 2026 it cost about 25 dollars per million Btu, the highest since Dec 2022. American ethane abroad: exports reached a record 794 thousand barrels a day in Aug 2026, and Europe's new cracker in Antwerp is built to use it. Europe's closures, Dow's Böhlen among them. Fertilizer: CF paid 3.31 dollars for its gas in 2025, up from 2.40; its margin rides on that number. PFAS: the limits, the settlements, and the lawsuits still open. And Germany's chemical output, which brings us to our call.
Called: Part twelve's forecast to test is the American government's own. In February 2005, the Energy Information Administration published its outlook to 2025. Gas was dear and getting dearer, so it expected America to import more and more of it as liquefied natural gas: 6.4 trillion cubic feet a year by 2025, up from 0.4. In 2025 America did the opposite. It exported 5.5 trillion cubic feet. Expecting dear gas, it cut its forecast for farm chemicals, nitrogen fertilizer among them, to growth of 0.6 per cent a year, because of foreign competition. American ammonia grew 2.3 per cent a year instead. For bulk chemicals it expected 1 per cent a year. The Federal Reserve's index of basic chemicals grew about 0.5 per cent, and plastics and resins about 0. Called it? On chemicals, roughly, and even a little high. On gas, the input that decides everything else, completely wrong: the outlook had not priced in shale.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. Germany's chemical output averaged 78.5 in 2025, on an index where 2021 is a hundred, and about 77 in the first nine months of 2026. We think that in 2027 it will still average below 79.8, at least twenty per cent below 2021. European gas was still about eight times America's price in September 2026, and the closures already announced take capacity out for good. Against us: gas could fall, demand could recover, and the figures get revised. We give it 75 per cent, and we will check it against Eurostat's figures in early 2028, right or wrong.
